source_evidence.observation: The paper defines 'whatever order of evaluation' for these updates as any rooted binary summation tree for c and the products a_i b_i; the surrounding division or square root remains part of the stated update form. (PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph following equations (1.5a)-(1.5c).)

The improved bounds replace gamma terms by constants linear in u, contain no O(u^2) term or dimension restriction, and apply with round-to-nearest for any radix, tie-breaking rule, dimension, and summation order when underflow and overflow are absent. (PDF p. 4, anchor: equation (1.8) and following summary paragraph.)

F is a symmetric set of finite floating-point numbers containing zero, with radix beta, precision p, and an exponent range; fl is round-to-nearest with unrestricted tie-breaking, and u = (1/2) beta^(1-p) <= 1/2. The page also defines the paper's underflow convention. (PDF p. 5, anchor: sections 2.1-2.2 and equations (2.1a)-(2.1b).)

source_evidence.anchor: notation paragraph at the end of section 3
source_evidence.observation: The paper writes a_ij for matrix entries and diag(f(i)) for the n by n diagonal matrix with diagonal entry f(i), with i implicitly ranging from 1 through n. (PDF p. 9, anchor: notation paragraph at the end of section 3.)

For a floating-point evaluation of (c - sum_{i=1}^{k-1} a_i b_i)/b_k with nonzero floating-point b_k, Lemma 4.1 gives perturbation constants bounded by k u; if b_k = 1 and no division occurs, the bound is (k-1)u. It allows any summation order and assumes no underflow or overflow. (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1.)

source_evidence.anchor: section 4.3 opening, Lemma 4.3, and Theorem 4.4 statement
source_evidence.observation: The section defines Cholesky factorization as computation of the upper-triangular factor by the conventional algorithm. Lemma 4.3 supplies the (k+1)u square-root-update constant. Theorem 4.4 assumes only a symmetric A in F^(n x n), successful completion, and absence of underflow and overflow, and identifies a computed factor R_hat in F^(n x n). (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening, Lemma 4.3, and Theorem 4.4 statement.)
Equation (4.4) states R_hat^T R_hat = A + DeltaA and the two componentwise bounds |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u)|R_hat^T||R_hat| <= (n+1)u|R_hat^T||R_hat|. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

source_evidence.anchor: conventional column-update formulas in the proof of Theorem 4.4
source_evidence.observation: The conventional algorithm computes R_hat one column at a time. For column j it evaluates y_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k=1}^{i-1} r_hat_ki r_hat_kj)/r_hat_ii for i = 1,...,j-1 and y_jj = (a_jj - sum_{k=1}^{j-1} r_hat_kj^2)^(1/2), with r_hat_ij and r_hat_jj denoting the computed values. (PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional column-update formulas in the proof of Theorem 4.4.)

For 1 <= i < j <= n, equation (4.5a) has constant i u and sums through k = i. For 1 <= j <= n, equation (4.5b) has constant (j+1)u and sums through k = j. The proof completes the full matrix bound using symmetry. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) and closing symmetry sentence.)

binders: n is the implicitly positive integer matrix dimension; the theorem does not restate n in N_{>0}, but its n by n dimensions and loops j = 1,...,n inherit that convention. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional column-update formulas.)
A ranges over symmetric matrices in F^(n x n), where each input entry is a finite floating-point number. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1.)

R_hat in F^(n x n) denotes the factor actually computed by the conventional Cholesky execution, rather than the exact Cholesky factor of A. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4 statement.)

DeltaA is the n by n backward perturbation fixed by DeltaA = R_hat^T R_hat - A; equation (4.4) presents it through the equivalent exact relation R_hat^T R_hat = A + DeltaA. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

The proof quantifies columns j = 1,...,n, off-diagonal row indices i = 1,...,j-1, and summation indices k with the bounds shown in the update and residual formulas. (PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas and equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
hypotheses: A is symmetric and floating-point-valued: A in F^(n x n). Positive definiteness is not a hypothesis of Theorem 4.4. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)
The conventional Cholesky factorization runs to completion on A. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement and section 4.3 opening.)
No underflow and no overflow occur during the execution. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)
Arithmetic uses the paper's standard finite floating-point system and rounding to nearest; ties may be broken by any rule. (PDF p. 5, anchor: sections 2.1-2.2.)

The summations inside the conventional updates may be evaluated in any order represented by a binary summation tree. (PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph following equations (1.5a)-(1.5c); PDF p. 12, anchor: paragraph introducing equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
conclusions: Exact backward relation: R_hat^T R_hat = A + DeltaA. The matrix products and subtraction in this relation are exact real operations on the completed floating-point data. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
First global bound: |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u) (|R_hat^T| |R_hat|), with diag indexed by i = 1,...,n. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4); PDF p. 9, anchor: diag notation paragraph.)

Second global bound: |DeltaA| <= (n+1)u (|R_hat^T| |R_hat|). This is the second inequality in the chain in (4.4), not a replacement for the row-dependent first inequality. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
Local off-diagonal estimate: for every 1 <= i < j <= n, |a_ij - sum_{k=1}^i r_hat_ki r_hat_kj| <= i u sum_{k=1}^i |r_hat_ki||r_hat_kj|. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5a) with the preceding j-loop.)
Local diagonal estimate: for every 1 <= j <= n, |a_jj - sum_{k=1}^j r_hat_kj^2| <= (j+1)u sum_{k=1}^j r_hat_kj^2. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5b) with the preceding j-loop.)

The local upper-triangular estimates are completed to a whole-matrix result using the symmetry of A - R_hat^T R_hat and the Gram-product structure. (PDF p. 12, anchor: closing symmetry sentence after equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
definitions_and_conventions: For symmetric positive definite real A, the section calls the unique upper-triangular R with positive diagonal and A = R^T R its Cholesky factor; 'Cholesky factorization' means computing R using the conventional algorithm. This section-level definition does not add positive definiteness to Theorem 4.4. (PDF p. 11, anchor: opening paragraph of section 4.3 and Theorem 4.4 statement.)
F is a symmetric set of finite floating-point numbers containing zero, with integer radix beta >= 2, precision p >= 1, and an exponent range. (PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1.)
fl rounds a real number to a nearest member of F when overflow does not occur, with no prescribed tie-breaking rule. (PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1.)
The unit roundoff is u = (1/2) beta^(1-p), hence u <= 1/2. (PDF p. 5, anchor: equations (2.1a)-(2.1b) and following paragraph.)
diag(f(i)) is the n by n diagonal matrix with entry f(i) in position (i,i), with i implicitly ranging from 1 to n. (PDF p. 9, anchor: notation paragraph at the end of section 3.)

In (4.4), bars on matrices denote entrywise absolute values, inequalities are entrywise, and juxtaposition |R_hat^T||R_hat| is ordinary matrix multiplication of the nonnegative absolute-value matrices; it cannot be a matrix norm because the row-scaling diagonal produces an n by n bound. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

Hatted entries are computed floating-point values, while the sums, products, squares, transpose, and residuals displayed in (4.4)-(4.5) are exact real expressions formed from those computed values. (PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas, equation (4.4), and equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
implicit_context: The output is upper triangular because the referenced conventional algorithm computes entries r_hat_ij for i <= j one column at a time; Theorem 4.4 itself records only R_hat in F^(n x n). (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening; PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional column-update formulas.)

Although the section introduces the exact Cholesky factor for symmetric positive definite matrices, the theorem deliberately weakens the matrix hypothesis to symmetry plus successful execution. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4 statement.)

Lemma 4.1 supplies the division-update constant k u for a nonzero denominator; its special no-division case has constant (k-1)u. The proof of Theorem 4.4 uses the division case to obtain the i u constant in (4.5a). (PDF p. 10, anchor: Lemma 4.1; PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5a).)

Lemma 4.3 supplies the square-root-update constant (k+1)u when the computed pre-square-root quantity is nonnegative; with k = j this yields the (j+1)u constant in (4.5b). (PDF p. 11, anchor: Lemma 4.3; PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5b).)
The exact perturbation DeltaA need not itself be floating-point-valued; it is an exact real matrix residual of the computed factorization. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
statement.algorithm_linkage: The result is tied to the conventional upper-triangular, column-oriented Cholesky method, not to an arbitrary Cholesky variant. For j = 1,...,n, after columns 1,...,j-1 are available, it evaluates y_ij = (a_ij - sum_{k=1}^{i-1} r_hat_ki r_hat_kj)/r_hat_ii for i = 1,...,j-1 and y_jj = (a_jj - sum_{k=1}^{j-1} r_hat_kj^2)^(1/2); r_hat_ij and r_hat_jj are the resulting computed values. Summation association may vary, but the column order, division placement, and square-root variant are fixed by these formulas. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening; PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional column-update formulas; PDF p. 3, anchor: definition of evaluation order.)
numerical_model: The model is standard finite floating-point arithmetic in radix beta and precision p with round-to-nearest, unrestricted tie-breaking, and unit roundoff u = (1/2) beta^(1-p). (PDF p. 5, anchor: sections 2.1-2.2.)

The input entries and computed factor entries belong to F; real products and sums appearing in the retrospective error equations are exact expressions involving those represented floating-point values. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.4)-(4.5).)

The conventional updates contain floating-point products, summations, divisions, and square roots, with all rounding effects absorbed into the computed entries and the stated residual bounds. (PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional column-update formulas and equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)

The theorem is valid for any radix, tie-breaking rule, dimension, and allowed summation order, subject to successful execution and absence of underflow and overflow. (PDF p. 4, anchor: summary paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)
error_notions: DeltaA is a backward error on the input matrix: the already computed R_hat is an exact factor of A + DeltaA. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
The global error bound is componentwise and relative to the computed-factor envelope |R_hat^T||R_hat|, rather than relative to A or to a scalar matrix norm. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

Equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) are scalar absolute residual bounds for individual off-diagonal and diagonal entries and are the local estimates from which the global backward bound is assembled. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) and closing symmetry sentence.)
norms: No vector or matrix norm occurs in Theorem 4.4. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
For matrices, |.| is entrywise absolute value and <= is componentwise order; |R_hat^T||R_hat| is a matrix product, not a Hadamard product or norm product. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
For the local estimates, |.| is ordinary scalar absolute value, while each right-hand sum is a nonnegative exact sum of absolute products or squares. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
constants_and_indexing: The diagonal scaling in the first global bound is diag((i+1)u) for i = 1,...,n, so its diagonal entries are 2u, 3u, ..., (n+1)u. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4); PDF p. 9, anchor: diag notation paragraph.)
The uniform global constant is exactly (n+1)u. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
For an off-diagonal position with 1 <= i < j <= n, the exact local constant is i u, and both sums in (4.5a) run from k = 1 through k = i. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5a).)
For a diagonal position j with 1 <= j <= n, the exact local constant is (j+1)u, and both sums in (4.5b) run from k = 1 through k = j. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.5b).)

The computational off-diagonal numerator sums only through i-1 before division by r_hat_ii, whereas its residual estimate sums through i after incorporating the newly computed term r_hat_ii r_hat_ij. (PDF p. 12, anchor: off-diagonal update formula and equation (4.5a).)

The computational diagonal radicand sums only through j-1 before square root, whereas its residual estimate sums through j after incorporating r_hat_jj^2. (PDF p. 12, anchor: diagonal update formula and equation (4.5b).)
higher_order_terms: Equation (4.4) is exactly linear in u and contains no u^2 term, O(u^2) remainder, gamma factor, or other omitted higher-order term. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4); PDF p. 4, anchor: summary following equation (1.8).)

There is no smallness hypothesis such as (n+1)u < 1 and no upper restriction on n beyond being a matrix dimension. (PDF p. 4, anchor: summary paragraph following equation (1.8); PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)
The local constants i u and (j+1)u in (4.5) are also exact stated bounds with no omitted higher-order terms. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
exceptional_values: Underflow and overflow must be absent throughout the successful factorization. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)

The paper defines underflow as rounding a real t in the subnormal range with fl(t) != t; floating-point addition cannot underflow under this convention, multiplication and division can, and square root cannot. (PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1.)

F contains only finite floating-point numbers; overflow may map outside F to an infinity, but that case is excluded by the theorem. (PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1; PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)

The theorem does not explicitly mention NaNs, signed zeros, zero divisors, or negative square-root arguments; such breakdowns are addressed only through the requirement that the conventional factorization run to completion. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas.)

Symmetric indefiniteness is not itself excluded syntactically: positive definiteness is not required if the floating-point execution nevertheless runs to completion. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4 statement.)

undebatable_constraints: The input hypothesis is symmetry of A in F^(n x n), not symmetric positive definiteness. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)

The algorithm is the conventional upper-triangular, column-at-a-time Cholesky method with the displayed division and square-root updates. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening; PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas.)
Successful completion and absence of both underflow and overflow are mandatory hypotheses. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement.)
The primary conclusion must include the exact equality R_hat^T R_hat = A + DeltaA. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
Both parts of the global bound must be preserved: the row-dependent diag((i+1)u) bound and the coarser uniform (n+1)u bound. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

The bound is componentwise and uses the computed-factor envelope |R_hat^T||R_hat|; replacing it by a norm bound, |A|, |R_hat^T R_hat|, or a Hadamard product changes the claim. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
The off-diagonal local bound has constant i u and sums through i, while the diagonal local bound has constant (j+1)u and sums through j. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b).)
The constants contain no gamma term, no u^2 or O(u^2) remainder, and impose no condition such as (n+1)u < 1. (PDF p. 4, anchor: summary following equation (1.8); PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)

Any-order language concerns the evaluation order of the sums inside the fixed conventional update formulas; it does not authorize an arbitrary Cholesky variant. (PDF p. 3, anchor: definition of evaluation order; PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas.)
The final passage uses symmetry to extend the local triangular-entry estimates to the complete matrix inequality. (PDF p. 12, anchor: closing symmetry sentence.)

ambiguities.issue: The phrase 'Cholesky factorization runs to completion' is not formally expanded into a complete list of breakdown conditions.
ambiguities.evidence: The theorem states successful completion as a hypothesis, while the displayed algorithm contains divisions by r_hat_ii and square roots of computed radicands; the passage does not separately enumerate zero-pivot, negative-radicand, invalid-operation, or final-zero-pivot cases. (PDF p. 11, anchor: Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 12, anchor: conventional update formulas.)
ambiguities.impact: The source contract must retain successful completion as an opaque execution hypothesis. It should not silently replace it by positive definiteness, by a particular family of pivot inequalities, or by only nonzero denominators.

ambiguities.issue: The exact scope of 'whatever the order of evaluation' is abbreviated in the theorem proof.
ambiguities.evidence: The proof says the displayed values are computed whatever the order of evaluation, while the earlier formal explanation defines this freedom through rooted binary trees for the summation part of expressions c - sum a_i b_i. (PDF p. 12, anchor: paragraph before equations (4.5a)-(4.5b); PDF p. 3, anchor: paragraph following equations (1.5a)-(1.5c).)
ambiguities.impact: The guaranteed freedom is arbitrary summation association inside each fixed update. The source does not thereby claim arbitrary column ordering, movement of division or square root, or equivalence for every Cholesky algorithm variant.

ambiguities.issue: The paper describes F as 'similar to' IEEE 754-2008 rather than giving a complete bit-level datatype specification.
ambiguities.evidence: Section 2.1 specifies finite F, radix, precision, exponent range, symmetry, zero, normal/subnormal ranges, and round-to-nearest behavior, but uses the phrase 'similar to those defined in the IEEE 754-2008 standard.' (PDF p. 5, anchor: section 2.1.)
ambiguities.impact: A formalization should rely on the stated floating-point and rounding properties, not add an unstated requirement that F be exactly one particular IEEE interchange format.

contract_plain_english: For any positive matrix dimension n and any symmetric floating-point matrix A, execute the conventional upper-triangular Cholesky algorithm one column at a time, allowing any summation order inside its fixed division and square-root updates. Assume that the execution runs to completion and that neither underflow nor overflow occurs; positive definiteness is not separately required. (PDF p. 11, anchor: section 4.3 opening and Theorem 4.4 statement; PDF p. 12, anchor: update formulas.) If R_hat is the computed floating-point factor, then in exact real arithmetic R_hat^T R_hat = A + DeltaA, where the componentwise backward error satisfies |DeltaA| <= diag((i+1)u)|R_hat^T||R_hat| <= (n+1)u|R_hat^T||R_hat|. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4); PDF p. 9, anchor: diag notation paragraph.) Locally, for 1 <= i < j <= n the off-diagonal residual is bounded by i u times sum_{k=1}^i |r_hat_ki||r_hat_kj|, and for 1 <= j <= n the diagonal residual is bounded by (j+1)u times sum_{k=1}^j r_hat_kj^2; symmetry completes the full matrix bound. (PDF p. 12, anchor: equations (4.5a)-(4.5b) and closing symmetry sentence.) All constants are exactly linear in u, with no gamma term, higher-order remainder, or dimension-smallness restriction. (PDF p. 4, anchor: summary following equation (1.8); PDF p. 12, anchor: equation (4.4).)
